dietEvidence.body: The beak and teeth indicate herbivory. No gut contents are known; the plants eaten and the feeding mechanics are inferred from anatomy.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A small ornithopod with a lightweight skull and long hindlimbs. Early reconstructions placed it in trees; the anatomy supports a primarily terrestrial animal.
summary: A small ornithopod with a lightweight skull and long hindlimbs. Early reconstructions placed it in trees; the anatomy supports a primarily terrestrial animal.

discovery.body: Named by Huxley, 1869. The record is known from Wessex Formation, Isle of Wight. Many partial skeletons from the Isle of Wight.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Multiple partial skeletons are known from the Wessex Formation, including skull and postcranial material. The hypodigm samples several individuals.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Wessex Formation, Isle of Wight records the species in the Early Cretaceous. The numeric range used here is ≈130–125 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The skull is small and lightweight, with a beak and teeth suited to cropping plants. The hindlimbs are long and the forelimbs short, consistent with a bipedal stance.

behaviour.body: The species is reconstructed as primarily terrestrial. Experimental tracks show how footprint shape changes with sand wetness, but they do not identify a wild trackmaker or record speed. No social behaviour is known.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from many partial skeletons from the Isle of Wight. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: Hypsilophodon is known from multiple partial skeletons from the Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight. The old arboreal reconstruction is not supported by its limb and foot anatomy. No gut contents are known.

primer.lead: Hypsilophodon foxii was a small, fast-running plant-eater from the [Wessex Formation](/prehistoric-world#worlds) of the Isle of Wight, England, during the [Early Cretaceous](/deep-time?period=cretaceous). It is one of the best-known small ornithopods.
paragraphs: The skull is lightweight, with a beak and teeth suited to cropping plants. The long hindlimbs and short forelimbs indicate a bipedal stance. Early reconstructions placed Hypsilophodon in trees, but later anatomical work treated it as primarily terrestrial.
Experimental footprints show how track shape changes with sand wetness, but they do not identify a wild trackmaker. No gut contents are known, and its social and nesting behaviour is unknown.
primer.takeaway: A small bipedal plant-eater, once wrongly imagined as a tree-dweller.
